Question: What were the reasons for Germany's defeat in World War II despite having superior weapons such as Panzer tanks and ME-109 fighters?
Answer: Imagine that you had an ideology that said left-handed people were the root of all your country’s problems. All you had to do to reach the pinnacle of your potential was to get rid of all the lefties. You devote enormous resources to this issue. and endlessly toil and moil over ambidextrous people and those who might be cunningly concealing their left-handedness. Then you start wars with pretty much anyone, because you have this right-handed purity thing, so you’re bound to win, right? It turns out what actually counts in war is not handedness, or racial purity, or any of that nonsense. The Nazis mad ideology prevented them from seeing what was actually clear to the Allies: having petrol, rubber, food, penicillin, tanks, planes and ships that can be mass produced and repaired in the field etc is what counts. Certainly the Germans had some spectacular weapons like the V2 rocket, the super-heavy Maus tank and the Messerschmitt 262 jet, but they were all costly flops, dazzling pieces of theatre that wasted valuable resources and only hastened Germany’s defeat. Btw, Churchill was a leftie.

Question: What changes in British society and culture have been most striking over the past 70 years?
Answer: I'm almost 70. When I was a kid in London, everyone smoked. Really everyone, including doctors. It was slightly unusual if an adult didn't. Now the reverse is true. No one picked up after their dog. You had to watch where you were walking. Everything is cleaner now. In the past, car ownership was very aspirational. I remember, as a car-mad youngster, ruthlessly judging adults on the car they drove. No one cares much now. National Service was expected. When the Conservatives floated the idea of bringing it back at the last election…well, let's just say it wasn't a vote winner. Murderers were still being hanged. No one (apart from a few extremists) wants that again. In fact people nowadays are much more likely to show understanding and pity when someone commits a crime. Children were labelled "stupid" for having what we now know are a wide range of learning disabilities. People were very deferential. If you look at old interviews of Harold Wilson by Robin Day, they were almost grovelling compared to the more provocative techniques used now. Parents didn't challenge their children's teachers. Now it's commonplace. People went to church. Now most of the population is atheist. People were not very socially mobile in the past. You stayed in your lane. We move up and down much more now. In the past, casual racism and sexism was normal. Now it's very much frowned upon. I don't remember liking my parents' taste in music much, but my kids like mine. I can't say they play the Beatles for instance, but the see merit in them. Seventy years ago, Britain was determined to export manufactured goods at all cost. It was very keen on doing business with Europe and wanted to cooperate with our closest neighbours and markets as much as possible. Now, sadly, Britain is more isolationist. Britain was a real world power, with the remnants of an empire and huge clout in the world. That's changed dramatically. In the 1950's it wasn't very common to see someone with dark skin. Now Britain is home to a huge range of cultures that all feed in to a very diverse mix.

Question: Why did people think putting carpeting in a bathroom in the 1950s was a great idea?
Answer: We didn’t have it, but I know people who did. It was simply because bathrooms were cold (in the UK at least) and getting out of a nice warm bath onto freezing lino or tiles wasn’t very nice. Carpet made the floor feel warmer, more cosy. It could be replaced cheaply because bathrooms were small.

Question: Senior citizens: What was your experience like in being a latchkey kid?
Answer: I grew up in London and went to school in the 1960’s and 70’s. My parents had shops so when I got home from school (by red double decker bus and walking) my parents were still at work. In my junior (prep) school I just got on with my homework, but after I was 11 I moved to a different type of school and had an avalanche of work in the evening…so much so that my parents tried letting me board at the school in the week (it was an hour travelling each way) and then they moved home so we lived much closer to my school. In time I got to grips with the homework volume and so when I arrived home, friends from school who lived nearby came to my house for tea and toast, free from adult and parental supervision. It was brilliant. We talked nonsense, played games, mucked about and were generally being teenagers until my mother got back at about 6pm. They all went home and I got on with my homework. I didn’t once regret being independent in this way. In fact I think it was great, and some of the mates I made in those happy days eating toast are still close friends.

Question: Is Labour turning Britain into a 'nanny state' with its proposed ban on smoking in public spaces?
Answer: There is an issue with banning smoking in public spaces, and that's coming from someone who lost both parents to smoking. When the ban on smoking in pubs was proposed, the argument was that smokers were forcing non-smokers to breathe their second hand smoke. I strongly supported that move. Smokers were made to go outside, and many establishments built areas where smokers could indulge, free from people like me waving away their smoke and doing pantomime coughing. The proposal to ban those isn't about second hand smoke. It's about stamping out smoking altogether in the U.K. The government has said as much. And this involves personal liberty, and raises the issue of other things people choose to do but which aren't in the best interests of their health, such as heavy drinking, motorbike riding, etc. Since we all pay into a pot for our healthcare, a healthy population will help to bring down long terms costs for the cash-strapped NHS. We all have an interest in that. So will we ban stag do's and Kawasakis next? What then? Ham sandwiches and pork pies? I don't know where I stand on this because I really hate smoking, but at the same time I think people should be free to run a high risk of killing themselves. Part of the human condition is to be stupid. Maybe add a "NHS contribution" on all tobacco products so that when smokers buy their tobacco they contribute a bit more for the treatment they may need. Maybe not though, because lung cancer is a cheap disease to treat, unlike dementia.

Question: If you could create a universal language that everyone could speak fluently, what would its core principles be?
Answer: I would make it phonetic like German, so every letter is pronounced. So no thought, thorough, through etc. Regarding spelling, in English we have 'four', fourteen' but 'forty'. That makes no sense. I'd make the spelling phonetic and consistent. I'd dispense with inanimate objects having genders. In fact nouns don't need genders at all. The languages that use gendered nouns are very inconsistent and they each need to be learned individually. They are often illogical. In German, Mädchen ("girl") is neuter, not feminine. (Hat doff to Jake Arnott). I would have different words for different things, so the context isn't so important. In English we have words like "Fast" which means to move quickly, but to "Hold fast" means to not move at all. The word "Ball" can mean a spherical object or a grand party with dancing. Other languages seem not to do this so much, although "Golf" in German means the game when it's neuter and "gulf" when masculine, and "See" can mean a lake as well as an ocean depending on its gender. I would make words descriptive. In English, men wear "Trunks" for swimming, but without "swimming" in front (and it's often omitted) a foreigner learning the language wouldn't be able to guess what is meant. In German, "Badehosen" literally means "Bathing trousers", which is simple and descriptive (although rather long). I'd also make the grammar absolutely consistent. No irregular verbs, and no weird tense changes. If you have "I go" changing to "I went" it just makes the past tense more difficult to anticipate. More regular would be "I gone" for instance. I would not have cases. In German there are four, and although it makes the language precise and rather beautiful, it also makes it hard for a foreigner to learn. I would dispense with the formal and informal. In English we have done this already, but in French and German they still retain it. In time I believe these languages will drop the formal/informal as well, and if I was starting from scratch I wouldn't bother. I would keep numbers reading from left to right as in English. In German, seventy-nine is "nine and seventy", and don't even get me started on French.

Question: For those age 60 and older, what were your first exposures to cannabis? Not necessarily using it, but hearing about it or learning of its existence. How did that shape your perspective?
Answer: I went to an exclusive all boys school in England and had no interaction with drugs. There were one or two who in retrospect had a connection to the sub-culture, but I didn't and nor did any of my friends. When I went to art college in central London, there were obviously people there who indulged, and I took the odd puff. However it really didn't do anything for me. I wanted it to, but as I didn't smoke tobacco, it just tasted of Smokey burnt leaves. Horrible. I coughed my guts up. Later in the advertising industry there was the obvious smell of cannabis in the creative department where I worked, but coke was the industry drug of choice in the 80's and 90's, so cannabis seemed somehow rather quaint. I tried coke once and liked it so much that I swore never to do so again, and I've stuck to that.

Question: Is it considered rude to speak a foreign language in front of a spouse who does not understand it?
Answer: It depends. By talking in the foreign language, you are in effect excluding the other person in your party who cannot speak that language, so you should do what you can to include them. One method would be to frequently pause and translate…in effect, be an interpreter. Furthermore, I wouldn't allow this conversation to persist for very long. Firstly, it's tiring being an interpreter, and secondly, this situation is always disjointed and not free-flowing, as normal conversation is. So if it's brief and you include your spouse, it's fine.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Growing up how common were working mothers among your peers?
Answer: I was born in the mid 1950's, and since my parents owned shops, Mum always worked along side my Dad. We weren't well off but my parents were very ambitious. She was unique. Amongst my friends in the 1960's and even '70's, none of the mothers worked. Not one. Even the ones who weren't well off and who obviously struggled to pay the private school fees. Mum did so proudly though, as together my parents built a good business that afforded our family a good lifestyle. Her contribution was a vital part of its success. My friends congregated after school at my house, happy to enjoy the freedom the absence of parental supervision gave us. The gaggle of teenage boys went home at 6pm when she arrived back from work. She liked seeing them and they thought she was great. Who knows what their parents thought? She was far too practical and pragmatic to care anyway. My parents were atypical. My brother was far more traditional in that he married a girl who didn't work. She had a small part time job for a while but he didn't encourage her. In the 80's and 90's that was not so unusual. My late wife had her own career and ran her own business from home when our three children were growing up in the 80's and 90's. We also had au pairs and house cleaners. For her, it was a matter of pride, independence and self-fulfilment. It wouldn't have occurred to her not to. But even then, where we lived in the prosperous London suburbs, it wasn't all that common. Her friends often said "You're amazing…I don't know how you do it all", but to women like her and my mother, "doing it all" was the only way they wanted to live. In a sense, they were both ahead of their time. My children have wives and partners who work and they would think it odd to do otherwise. My eldest son's wife is I believe the main earner in their family. she runs her own successful and growing company while his job allows him the flexibility to be a hands-on Dad.

Question: Jimmy Savile looks like a stereotypical creep. How did British people fall for his weirdo act for so long?

The BBC chose to turn a blind eye to the muttering about him for their own selfish reasons. I was a teenager as Saville emerged on our screens and always found him unappealing, talentless and just weird. I didn't know anyone who thought otherwise but presumably the out of touch BBC saw him as a "madcap" and therefore likely to appeal to youngsters. In those deferential times, establishment was not scrutinised as it is today.

Question: What is the purpose of having an afternoon tea? What are the benefits of holding one? Are there any etiquette rules associated with it?
Answer: In the UK it’s a much less formal thing than it once was. For the average person it’s usually no more than a mug of tea (made with a teabag) and something sweet (a chocolate biscuit will do) while there is a brief pause in whatever activity happens to be occurring. It doesn’t require company. That’s what it usually is for me at any rate, but I grew up in London and in other regions it’s different. I find it nicely fills the void after lunch and gives me a little boost until supper time. It is often accompanied by aimlessly staring out of the window. Regarding the rules, for me it is boiling the water in the kettle and removing the well-brewed teabag before adding the milk. Obviously. I’m not a complete barbarian.

Question: How can parents handle a picky child who refuses to eat healthy foods? Have you found any long-term solutions to this issue?
Answer: Children go through phases, and for several years one of my sons ate virtually only fish fingers and peas. Ok, that’s not too bad nutritionally, but in time he just grew out of it. I don’t think it did him any harm. He’s grown normally, his teeth are great, he’s a father himself, etc etc. So my take on it is to relax and not to let the media panic you into thinking that your child is being malnourished. They probably aren’t, but it’s tedious and boring for you. Try sighing, rolling your eyes and file it under “Things to bring up when they bring a partner home”.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do you think the Nazis "felt guilt" over the Holocaust?
Answer: The evidence from Nazis such as Adolf Eichmann suggest that they wanted to complete their appointed task of murdering all of Europe's Jews. They felt guilty that they were inefficient and failed in their task. Only those who feigned ignorance such as Albert Speer expressed regret for the mass murder. So guilt is a moot point. On one hand we have no acknowledgment of a crime, and on the other hand we have the denial of knowledge. Where does guilt fit into this? To feel guilt you have to accept you've done something wrong. I can't think of a well-known Nazi who ever actually achieved this, but I met one once. I was at the beer fest in Munich in the late 1970's and got chatting to an older man. He asked me about where I was from. I told him that I was born in London, the son of a Jewish refugee from Vienna. We were both a bit pissed tbh, but the guy was in tears on hearing this. He told me he had been a Nazi and had seen and done things he now deeply regretted. He was now a committed Christian. He felt only shame as a German, and was amazed that I should feel comfortable living in Germany. We exchanged addresses and a few weeks later he sent me some opals to have set into a necklace for my wife. I hate to think what he did to make this gesture necessary, but he was a guilty man if ever I saw one, and his guilt was a heavy burden.

Question: What do you think of proposals to increase the penalties in the UK for parents who take their children out of school during term time to get cheaper holidays?
Answer: I think schooling is vital, and I'm sure pretty well all parents agree. I also think that children benefit from experiences outside school, and this includes holidays, especially foreign ones. I find it sad that holiday firms, airlines, hotels etc penalise parents for wanting to go on holiday at the same time…a time that is enforced on them by schools. I know, supply and demand, free enterprise, etc etc, but still. Bringing up kids is an expensive business these days and most parents can do without being exploited by airlines just for adhering to the school rules. I therefore propose that airlines, hotels etc shouldn't be allowed to crank up their charges as soon as schools break up. Keep them at a sustainable average, so that parents aren't tempted to take their children out of school early and the holiday industry can still make their profits.

Question: What is the general attitude of the British public towards immigration, particularly towards Syrian refugees?
Answer: I cannot speak for the British public, but I am sympathetic to any refugee. Being forced to leave your home country is not a lifestyle choice. It's a very hard road. Britain has a tradition of being welcoming to refugees that goes back centuries and they have always assimilated and brought benefits to Britain and British culture. With some who come from countries quite different from ours, this process might take a few generations, but it always happens. I note that under the last government, it took a long time for refugees to be processed. Keen to put obstacles in the way of refugees in order to deter them, the government purposely made the procedure slow. This made some very determined and motivated people desperate enough to risk their lives in small dinghies. This in turn has caused some hostility in the UK. We've seen it in the extreme form of far-right rioting in our cities. Personally, I would far rather have a determined refugee bent on making a success of his life in Britain than a chanting, violent right-wing extremist. I speak from experience. My fathers family were refugees. They were all successful because like many in their position, they had something to prove. One uncle was even knighted and became Lord, then Baron Schon. Others became professionals, served in the military etc. My father was a successful businessman, employing people and paying a lot of tax in his lifetime. Not one had a criminal record or had anything more than a speeding ticket. Nevertheless, in every cohort there are a few disappointing individuals, and refugees in general are no exception. However being kind to strangers is a tradition that goes to the heart of what it means to be British and it does a disservice to that if it is forgotten. The thugs we saw recently hurling abuse and rocks at Police protecting law and order may flatter themselves that they are patriots, but they are the very opposite.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Were British people concerned about a potential German invasion during World War II? If so, what measures did they take to prepare for it?
Answer: On the south coast of the U.K. there remain plenty of reminders of constructions designed to stall an invasion. I took this shot of "Dragons Teeth" near Poole recently. They are meant to stop tanks, or at least to channel them into killing fields. The south of England is littered with WW2 "pill box" machine gun nests. These brick and concrete bunkers were quickly erected all over the places where a landing by sea or air might conceivably occur. Beaches were guarded and mined. Cliffs were manned by lookouts and were covered in wire. So whilst no imminent invasion was ever expected, measures were taken. The public were concerned obviously, but my mother, born in London in 1920 said that she didn't ever lose sleep over it. My father, a child refugee from Vienna, did however. He had witnessed the Nazis in person and knew their zeal and ingenuity better than he knew the channel and the Royal Navy.

Question: If a woman's choice to abort a fetus is supposed to be hers totally, why can't that same woman choose to have a total hysterectomy at any age after 18 for any reason?
Answer: I know someone who had herself sterilised in her 20's. She was sure she didn't want kids. Now in her late 60's, she has no regrets. Why would that be anyone else's business? A hysterectomy is a big deal and no one needs to opt for that if all you want is confidence that you'll not get pregnant.

Question: What is the role of parents in providing healthy meals for their children? Should they have the authority to force their children to eat certain foods?
Answer: I've found that if children are only presented with healthy food, that is what their palates will become used to and that is what they will like. My daughter is quite hot on this. Her three children eat a variety of pretty healthy foods and it's what they consider to be normal. I've never seen them with a McDonald's, and although pizza is a favourite, the toppings are always very heavy on the vegetables. The kids all snack on raw vegetables and don't get things like sweets or chocolate very often. They love ice cream, but it's a treat. My eldest son does the same with his children. They're all very well fed, and none of them are 'forced' to eat this way. Because it's how they were brought up, it's what they know and like.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What was your favourite place that you have visited so far in Germany?
Answer: I recently visited Miniatur Wunderland in Hamburg, and right now it's my favourite place in Germany. It's the number one visitor attraction in Germany and has been for the last six years. It's the world's largest model train set. It cost €45million and is constantly expanding. Tbh, one runs out of superlatives describing this amazing model. It's vast. It's computer controlled, mad and it's hilarious. A you walk around the huge displays (arranged in countries) the lighting turns from night to day. In the display featuring Hamburg, there's a model of the building you're in with a model of the model inside. The model airport has planes taking off and landing. The area depicting Monaco shows the Grand Prix and has F1 cars racing through the streets. Like everything, even their speed is to scale. Amazing as the trains are, in a way it's the other things that amazed me. I loved the Shuttle taking off, the volcano, the airport, the seven murders (spot them if you can amongst the millions of tiny figures…I found only one), the ships moving around the water in the model of Scandinavia, the lovers in the field of sunflowers with Cupid hovering over them … Once inside the display you can stay all day if you want. There's no rush. You can go back and forth and take as many pictures as you like. Stunning and utterly joyous. Everyone there had a big smile on their face.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is the most amazing thing you overheard because people didn't think you understood their language?
Answer: I was being interviewed by two elderly sisters who owned an apartment block in Darmstadt, Germany. I wanted to rent one of the flats and they wanted to see if I was suitable. This was in the late 1970’s. So they asked me about my work (advertising) and that of my wife (ballet dancer in the Darmstadt Theatre …they were very impressed by that). Finally they asked me where I was from because they could detect a foreign accent, so I told them I was English, from London. One turned to the other and said quietly and quickly in the strong local accent (which I happened to understand quite well) “He’s ok, they’re almost like us”. What I didn’t know at the time was that Darmstadt was almost completely destroyed by the RAF in the war. The firestorm burned the house that stood where ours was, and all the others in the street. The sisters told me later about it, and it was pretty hair-raising. I thought it quite nice of them to say I was almost like them, although I wasn’t at all. They meant well even if their attitudes were rather typical of the era in which they grew up.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: My mom is cheating on my dad. I told my dad about it. My mom is mad and she said they're fighting because of me. She said that I should say goodbye to my college next year. Did I do the right thing? What should I do?
Answer: No, you interfered in the business of others. You shouldn't have done so. Discretion was called for and you chose to blurt out something that has done a lot of damage. Why? What good has it done? There is nothing you can do now apart from telling your parents you love them both equally, regardless. When I was a teen I discovered my father's affair. I did nothing except letting him know I knew. In time my parents marriage ended, but I didn't destroy it. He did. I believe I behaved correctly. In truth, a third person can only very rarely fully understand someone else's marriage. You don't know how your parents behave in private, what their physical relationship is, what their deep needs are etc, and you have no right to apply your morals on their relationship.

Question: What are some talents or hobbies that society values but you do not find interesting? Why do you not find them interesting?
Answer: I live in a country strewn with golf courses. Most of my friends play golf. Several are Chairmen of their cubs even. The son of one of my friends builds golf courses for a living. In the UK, golf is almost a national pastime. I’m completely indifferent to it though. This probably stems from the fact that my Dad didn’t play. He was Jewish, and although he was invited to join a club, when he found out that they had a Jewish quota, he refused despite being told that ‘they’ll let you in’. “Fuck them and their stupid little balls” he said.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do you like others seeing you naked?
Answer: I went to my best local beach today, which happens to be a naturist beach. It was a lovely day, the like of which we don’t often get in the UK, so I stripped off like everyone else. I had a skinny-dip in the surprisingly warm sea, and by the time I was back on my towel, I was dry. Remarkable. So the whole thing seemed very natural to me. I didn’t like others seeing me naked particularly but that wasn’t the point of the exercise. Letting the sun get to me completely and enjoying the rare feeling of freedom was the point, and very nice it was too. It didn’t feel at all weird or voyeuristic.

Question: Should I start ballet despite being a boy?
Answer: Probably not, because you display a weird attitude. If you’re interested in ballet, surely you must know that lots of boys do it, that it requires extreme physical fitness and strength, and is in fact very ‘manly’. So if you don’t know this, you’re obviously a bit ignorant about ballet and hung up on the outdated notion that there’s something effeminate about it. To you it seems that being ‘a boy’ is an obstacle. Well it isn’t. In fact it’s an advantage, because the female dancers have to do more work. However you’d be a team player in a dance company if you ever got that far, and your quaint ideas would be a bit of a problem. So for all these reasons, you’d be better off as a drag queen. That’s a thing only boys can do.

Question: Can an adult person learn how to dance ballet (or another type of dancing) without prior training in childhood?
Answer: Can they learn ballet? Yes. Will they be any good? No. Other types of dance vary in their demands and I expect some non-athletic types are pretty undemanding for an adult to master. I’m thinking of Morris dancing for instance, which requires some musical hopping and a decent memory, but that’s about it.

Question: What's the unique food you discovered whilst travelling?
Answer: In Mexico as a 17 year old I discovered Pollo y Mole. It’s chicken in a chilli and chocolate sauce, which sounds…unusual, but is in fact outstandingly brilliant.

Question: What is the purpose of a "pilot" episode in a TV series? Why do some shows not start with episode 1?
Answer: Pilot episodes are usually made to test audience reaction before the series is made. If it bombs, not much money has been lost, and if it shows promise but there are some wrinkles, these can be addressed when the series is made.

Answer: I’ve tried other things in my tea, and milk was the best….much better than vinegar, paraffin, iron filings, sausages or tuna fish, at any rate.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it considered acceptable for parents to make their children finish all the food on their plate, regardless of how much they have already eaten?
Answer: No, I think that's a rather old-fashioned way to bring up children. I'm not advocating waste but getting kids to eat and enjoy their meals doesn't have to be stressful and you don't need to be authoritarian. Just prepare what they like (I know this can be tedious…my eldest son lived on fish fingers and peas for several years) but providing they have something approaching a balanced diet, no harm will come to them. Bullying them and making meal times stressful is however a recipe for doing them harm. If they're full, they're full. Don't make it a battle of wills. Let them graze sometimes. The sky won't fall in.

Question: Is it worth pursuing a career as a professional ballet dancer if you dislike ballet but love to dance?
Answer: If you dislike ballet, why would you even want to be a professional ballet dancer? Loving dance is beside the point.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What factors led to Britain's victory over Germany during World War II, despite having a similar military force to France?
Answer: Well the obvious huge factor that allowed Britain fight on and not be invaded was the Channel and the Royal Navy which guarded it. Despite losing vast quantities of equipment on the Dunkirk beach, the British were pretty well invulnerable and the Germans could not take their continental victory further. While France and every other country in the west of Europe fell to Germany, Britain didn't because the Germans couldn't get to it. After that, the British and troops of the Empire fought on in North Africa and then the Far East when America joined in somewhat belatedly. After Germany attacked the USSR, Germany was pretty well doomed. The resources Britain was allied with were many times greater than those of France.

Name: Nick Schön

Question: If you travel to another country, what are the usual things you think of?
Answer: I go on a road trip in Europe every summer. It usually lasts a month, so I need quite a few summer clothes but also one warm outfit and one rain jacket, just in case. I move around a lot and have very limited space, so I have to travel light. I usually stay in one place for a while so I can wash and dry my kit at least once. I prepare meticulously by researching my route and what I want to see, what roads I want to drive down etc. I book airB&Bs and hotels in advance, but always opt for places I can cancel if need be. I often meet friends along the way and take them for a section of the trip with me, letting them out at a convenient airport or train station. Obviously I think too about money, the car, security etc. I usually have emergency backups for things. For example I seem to be a genius for leaving plug adapters in hotels (a UK electrical plug is different to the ones used in the rest of Europe) so I take several. I make sure my car insurance is covering me for abroad (it always does, but I always check). I always also check my breakdown cover is international. I have never had to use it but again, I always calm my natural anxiety by double-checking. This is my favourite road trip car. I stupidly sold it a year ago and bought an '81 911 Targa which turned out to be a complete pos. I've sold it and intend getting another 356 like the one I sold. This year I've already had one trip with a friend in his car. I'm planning a second trip in September.

Question: What is the reason for tanks being heavy even though they are primarily used for running over things rather than long distance driving like cars or trucks?
Answer: Tanks are heavy because they are armoured and have a big gun. The ammo is heavy too, so as this all weighs many tons, it needs a big engine. That's heavy too. So is the fuel that big engine drinks. The weight of a tank is not necessarily desired. Tanks don't need to be heavy to be good tanks and driving over things to crush them isn't what they are intended for. In fact the super heavy tanks the Germans had and planned in WW2 like the Panzer VIII "Maus" weighing in at 188 tons were completely impractical because of their weight. Railways couldn't transport them to the front lines, they were too heavy for bridges and the ground they ran on wouldn't support them. If they broke, they'd be too heavy to recover, let alone fix. In contrast, the Allies' Sherman tank was 30–38 tonnes depending upon variant and was easy to transport, maintain and repair. Sure, they were vulnerable to German guns but if they knocked out ten, we always replaced them with eleven.

Question: Are Germans still Nazis today? How did Germans turn overnight into Nazis in WW2?

At its peak, membership in the Nazi Party (NSDAP) reached about 8.5 million people by 1945. Given that the population of Germany around that time was approximately 70-80 million, this means roughly 10-12% of the German population were members of the Nazi Party. So party membership wasn't even very widespread, and if you discount those who became members to keep their jobs rather than through conviction, the number of true Nazi loyalists shrinks even more. Question: Can you describe the process of building a home in England?
Answer: Find a plot and buy it. Design your house and apply for planning permission. Find a contractor once permission has been granted. Build. Apply for the VAT refund on building materials. This, in an idealised nutshell is how it is supposed to happen. Most people stumble on the first point because finding a plot that either already has planning permission or is likely to get it, is hard. Depending on where in the country you intend living it's usually between difficult and extremely so. Designing a house for your needs and budget can be a fun exercise and finding a good architect is key. Some Councils have been reluctant to grant planning. Some do so, but only if the design is virtually identical to surrounding properties. Most take a long time to consider your plans. If they reject them you can appeal but this also takes months and costs. The current government has said it will speed up the planning process. That is very much needed. Finding a good contractor is difficult too. Some are good and are therefore busy. You'll need to agree a cost and time and secure it with contracts. There are lots of unreliable and unscrupulous "builders" in the U.K. It's unregulated. Building needs to comply with building regulations and needs to be inspected at stages during the build. VAT does not apply to building materials but you have to pay it and then apply for a refund once the house has been finished. There is a strict protocol for doing this.

I owned a holiday home in Tenerife for about ten years and because it was in a place where the locals all spoke good English, I didn't learn. Question: What are the main differences between driving on British roads and American roads, besides left-sided traffic?
Answer: We have a lot of roundabouts. Americans call them "traffic circles" and they are not unknown there of course, but in the U.K. they are everywhere. There are even a few roundabouts arranged around a roundabout and one can travel in both directions around it. Hemel Hempstead is the proud owner of what is locally known as "The Magic Roundabout". If I were you I'd avoid that if possible or you'll get a nosebleed just trying to figure it out. I'm reliably informed by American relatives that we drive at "terrifying" speeds. Since UK roads are considerably safer than US roads and speed is a common cause of accidents, I doubt this is in fact true, but it might seem that way because our roads are so much narrower. Each lane is narrower and so vehicles are closer together. This is another issue for US drivers. Fine judgement is often called for. Where I live there are some rural roads wide enough for only one car. Meet a vehicle coming towards you and one of you will have to reverse to a slightly wider bit of road. Even then it will be a squeeze. That brings me to another point. Politeness is required. Courtesy is necessary. If someone lets you out in traffic or reverses to let you pass, it is normal to do a little wave, flash your headlights or let your hazard lights blink once to thank the other motorist. As a rule, observe what others do and copy their tone. Don't be aggressive behind the wheel. You may have to be assertive in order to make progress but don't be a dick and block junctions. Drive defensively as a rule. Err on the side of caution. Avoid using the horn. A gentle "toot" is the most that is ever needed and is quite a strong statement in the U.K. At what we call "zebra crossings" the motorist has to stop if someone is waiting to cross. School buses don't just stop in the middle of U.K. streets. They pull over to the side of the roads so the children can safely disembark. It's quite ok to pass a stationary school bus on the right. If you get pulled over by a traffic policeman you will be greeted by someone who might have had a hard day but won't be nasty or violent. You may get a telling off but usually it will be administered with good humour and certainly politeness. If you get a ticket, pay it and move on. Horses have right of way. I'm sure I've missed other points of difference. But courtesy, mimicking the tone of the other road users and not being a dick will get you quite a long way.

Question: After WWII, were there a lot of former pilots who never flew again in civilian life? It seems like that would be very depressing, going from such glory to something like a milk truck driver. How many left-over pilots were there?

The man wanted nothing more than to quietly sit in the back of the shop painstakingly stroking on layers of varnish to get a perfect, smooth finish. He hardly ever spoke, and at the end of the day he would just pack up his things and go home without a goodnight even. His work was flawless, and I often sat with him, just watching. My Dad had told me not to speak to him because he had a bad stutter, and I noticed that when he stopped the slow, repetitive action, his hands fluttered and trembled so he could barely button his coat. He was friendly and he showed me small acts of kindness, like making me a mug of tea when he made one for himself. Apparently he had been a rear gunner in a Halifax bomber and had spent most of a whole tour terrified out of his mind. He was taken off operations after his plane was badly shot up one night. He simply couldn't climb into the plane the next evening. So it seemed that what we romantically think of as "glory" was no such thing. It was terrifying enough to break some strong young men.

Question: Do people who speak multiple languages just translate the words back to their native tongue to understand it?
Answer: When I was learning German (in Germany - I'm a Londoner by birth) I realised that a threshold had been passed when the German word for something came more quickly than the English. I wasn't thinking in English or German…thoughts are pretty abstract (or maybe just mine are), but my wife and I basically started speaking a hybrid language we called "Germish" even when we were speaking English. Some German words are very specific and precise and describe something for which English doesn't cater. There is of course "Schadenfreude", that has now widespread usage in England, but there are many others, such as "Torschlussangst" or "Torschlusspanik" (meaning the fear of a window of opportunity closing, such as the prime time for becoming a parent). In other examples, German is just very economical, using one compound word where a phrase or sentence would be needed in English. "Wetterfühligkeit" means 'feeling under the weather' and suggests that it's a genuine and recognised condition that people could get time off work for. German is particularly good at providing words for the human condition which English ignores. So no, I don't think necessarily in English or in German, but sometimes one word just jumps into my mouth more quickly because the language caters for the thought better. As for translating the word or phrase back into my native language…rarely. Sometimes I have to do this with long sentences with intricate grammatical constructions but by and large, no.

So my friend (who is quite well off) simply bought a warehouse nearby to put everything in. Only that vast space is now crammed full too now. I tease him about it. His wife rolls her eyes. He just laughs and agrees. What a problem for his kids when he croaks! Until then, he's a happy hoarder, and tbh, what harm is he doing?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Another Tory has brainlessly tried to make money by cheating the bookies on the date of the election. What's happened to the tories? At one time they were expert at hiding their dodgy deals from the public. The country deserved better than this!
Answer: Can it get any worse for the Tories? If ever there was a worn out, rotten, falling apart government it must surely be this one. They obviously don't care any more…the terrible, desperate policies, the resignations, the bungled interviews, the unforced errors, the senior staff trying to just take the money and run because they know the game's up and they'll never get another chance…it's almost funny. Name: Nick Schön
Question: What work secret did you accidentally find out that changed everything?
Answer: I was a creative working for an excellent ad agency, but in their Frankfurt office, which was considered to be something of a backwater. I had done some work which had been noticed in London, which was the head office and probably the best creative agency in the world at the time. Anyway, they offered me a job there. It was the kind of career-forging opportunity that doesn't happen twice. Of course I was very flattered, but also terrified. Could I step up to the incredibly high levels of work they demanded? One day I was chatting to a seasoned American art director who had been sent over to round off his career in Germany before retiring. I liked him, and decided to reveal my anxiety to him. "Nick, are the people who made you this offer idiots?" He asked. ""Of course not! They are bloody genius'!" I replied. "So have faith in their judgement. If they thought you couldn't handle it, they wouldn't have made you the offer". That was reassuring. But I told that I felt I just didn't know enough yet and that this was too early in my career. "Look. In this business no one knows anything. You're being hired for your taste, not for your knowledge or experience. It's about who you are. Take the damn job or you'll regret it all your life". I took the job and was there for fifteen years. It worked out great.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is the best sports car for a young person with limited money?
Answer: Get a Mazda MX-5 (Miata in the US). It's superb fun, and being a Mazda, super well built. There are loads of them around so they aren't expensive and you'll have a huge choice. A simply brilliant little sports car.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it morally wrong for Polish people to hate Germans over WW2? Why or why not?
Answer: It ended almost 80 years ago. All the perpetrators are dead, and so are many of their sons and daughters. Europe is facing new threats and issues. What is the point of keeping old enmities alive at the expense of dealing with new problems? I'm all for remembering the past and honouring the victims, but I see no virtue in hating Germans now.

Question: What have you inherited that is better than money?
Answer: Common sense, although I don't have as much of it as they did. My Mum (born 1920 in London) and my Dad (born 1930 in Vienna) were really practical people who did what they had to do to make good lives for us. As a result, we became prosperous. Sadly they blew the results of their hard work and good judgement by the time they died, but what I inherited was worth more than wealth.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why was it easy for the Allies to trick the Germans in World War II?
Answer: A lot has been written about the tricks the Allies played on Germany and how they fell for Operation Mincemeat for instance. But not so much is known about German deception, some of which worked really well. Whole towns were created next to real towns so that they would divert night bombers. They were very effective. This is just one example. A lake was covered and a fake road created on it to disguise it from the air, fires were lit to divert bombers after the first wave had passed…in the era when precision bombing was virtually impossible, it wasn't so hard to trick opponents, especially at night.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Are you feeling disillusioned with Labour and considering not voting?
Answer: Labour hasn't been in power for…how many years exactly? A long time, at any rate. So no, I'm not in the least 'disillusioned with Labour'. I want to give them a crack at sorting out the shit the Tories made and turning a country I rather like back into one that commands some respect and that others admire. In time I might feel disillusioned, but I'm way off there right now.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are the potential benefits of buying a new car from an individual instead of a dealer?
Answer: Dealers often don’t have much wriggle room on the price. They have their overheads. A private seller isn’t in that position and you’ll probably be able to negotiate a better price. You’ll only be in competition with others their ad has attracted. You can still get an independent survey done if you like (although this will cost you of course). Lots of garages will do this. So the risk will be the same. An independent survey will be likely to reveal obvious flaws and you won’t have to rely on dealer bs. By buying from the actual owner you can ask all pertinent questions about the history of the car and how it’s been treated. You’ll see it in its home, so you’ll be able to judge. Buy it from a dealer and all that information will be erased. It will look it’s best, but that won’t tell you anything.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Are exotic cars considered impractical? Why do people buy exotic cars like Lamborghinis if they don't plan on using their full performance capabilities?
Answer: Exotic cars are not impractical if you consider the job for which they are intended. This isn't doing the shopping, helping a friend move house, towing a boat etc. They are designed to make the owners feel very special, to impress others and to deliver a unique driving experience. Your average Lamborghini is quite superbly practical if that's your definition.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it common for adults to lose touch with their friends due to changes in people's lives over time?
Answer: Of course. Jobs, partners, kids etc all become primary things in someone's life and take up a lot of time. People change as well. I'd say it's more unusual to have friends all one's life. Last week I had lunch with two friends I met when we were 11. We are 69 now. Although there were eras when we didn't meet for years, we were in touch through all the dramas of life, just keeping tabs on each other via maybe just a Christmas card with a scribbled note. Now we have all retired and have more time, we meet quite often. I'm meeting them again next month in fact when another old school friend is coming to London from his home in Dubai…he's not coming just for lunch of course, but it's a good opportunity. A few other close friends from that early period have drifted away, not to return. That's normal.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Should someone believe their partner if they say they will never forget their past love while being in a relationship with them?
Answer: It's normal to remember people for whom one has intense feelings. That's not being unfaithful or disloyal, it's just a fact of life. It's not a good sign to constantly refer to the memory though, and a wise partner doesn't cross-question them about it.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are the reasons for purchasing an expensive sports car instead of a cheaper used car or using public transportation?
Answer: A car is more than just a mode of transport. The more impractical the car, the truer that is, so an expensive sports car is not in competition with a bus.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are some cultural norms and customs that tourists should be aware of before traveling to Germany?
Answer: Germans don't smile as much as some nationalities do. Depending on where you come from, you might interpret this as being rude or even hostile, but that would be wrong. It's just not so much the norm in German culture. Germans are pretty relaxed about sex, nudity and bodily functions generally. So in a sauna, even a mixed public one, you'll be asked to leave if you're not naked. In an apple wine bar in Sachsehausen, Frankfurt that I used to go to, there was a vomitorium in the cellar. "Scheisse" is used so commonly it isn't really rude. The pedestrian lights are taken very seriously. Don't cross on a red man or you'll get some pretty nasty stares, some serious tutting or someone will start haranguing you. If there's a policeman there you'll get a bollocking and a fine. If in doubt, follow what you see others doing. Be nice, patient and friendly and you'll be fine. Politely ask someone if you need help. Most speak a bit of English and a surprising number speak it better than some Brits I've met.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why were British sports cars from the 1960s so underpowered and slow? In the US you could buy a 1967 L88 Corvette with a 427 cubic inch engine making 560 HP normally aspirated.
Answer: Obviously the Astons and Jaguars were not underpowered or slow, but the little MGs, Triumphs and Healys were built for a different market. They had old fashioned iron block, four or at best six cylinder engines and they were built on a budget. They were as fast as they could be made to be with the technology of the time. Even Italian cars like the Alfa Romeo Duetto, with its fabulous twin OHC engine was not much faster, although they were technically far more advanced. So comparing a Triumph TR4 or an MGA to a Corvette is not really fair. Compare a Corvette to an E-Type Jag and I'm pretty sure the Jag would more than hold its own. I know which I'd rather own.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What causes neighbourhoods to change over time? Is it possible for a good neighbourhood to turn bad, or for a bad neighbourhood to turn good? If so, how long does it typically take for these changes to occur?
Answer: In my lifetime great swathes of London have moved upmarket. When I lived in Clapham in south London in the 1970's it was a dump. I could afford to live there as an impoverished art student. But now it's terrific and so gentrified that a lot of quite high-earning people working in finance can't afford to live there. And it's the same for many other areas. This has happened because not nearly enough homes have been built in London, so people have moved into central but crappy areas and poured money into refurbishing run-down Victorian houses. Then the nice cafés and bars moved in and bingo, you have Islington, but minus the rats and the damp. You could argue that this is a good thing. But having a one bed flat in Lewisham (not central or very smart) costing close to £300,000 to buy or £1400 a month rent is not good. It means ordinary people like firemen, teachers, nurses etc are priced out of the market. The cost of travel in London makes that worse. London has a truly superb public transport system, but visitors are staggered at the cost.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are the pros and cons of having one large city compared to multiple small cities in the same country/state/region?
Answer: The U.K. has one really big city, London. It dominates the country and despite attempts to move organisations like the BBC away, it has a huge magnetic draw of finance and talent, to the detriment of other parts of the country. Sure, there's Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester, Bristol etc but they don't compare to London. This distorts property prices and the costs of doing business. It sucks resources from the regions. Germany has Berlin, but it is a federal republic and the regions all have their big cities. Compared to Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich, Stuttgart, Hamburg, Cologne are all pretty big and important. This seems more balanced and although Berlin is a big draw, so are other big cities.

Question: What are the benefits of allowing foreigners into a country if they do not speak the native language, especially when there are already many people in the country who are looking for work and do speak the language?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: I’ve never seen a man who isn’t rich have a woman smiling with him, and appreciating him. Do you think women like men who are broke?
Answer: Admittedly, being skint is not an attractive quality in itself, but being rich isn’t necessarily either, except to a certain type of person. Most of us are neither skint nor loaded though. The vast majority of us are somewhere between getting by and being comfortably off, and when it comes to finding partners we tend to find that the size of our bank balance doesn’t really make a huge difference. Mostly people find partners in a similar income bracket to themselves, and that equanimity seems sensible.

Question: Do adult immigrants forget their native language after living in another country for years and raising children there?
Answer: My Dad left Austria when he was 8 in 1938 and lived the rest of his life in London. He spoke perfect English without an accent and avoided speaking his native language. In fact I can only remember hearing him speaking German to a few aged aunts who couldn’t speak English. All the rest of the time the Austrian side of my family all spoke English together even when they were not with an English member of the family (like my mother) who spoke no German. However my father and I spoke German to each other on a few occasions. I can’t remember why. I learned my German in Frankfurt in the 1970’s and 80’s, and noticed his Austrian accent and rather quaint turn of phrase. He spoke it quite perfectly though.

Question: Was the ‘Get Brexit Done’ slogan a vote-winner for the Tories in 2019? If so, then why have the Tories barely mentioned Brexit at all during the 2024 election campaign? Shouldn’t they be proudly running on the fact that they indeed got Brexit done?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How do I self-discipline and motivate myself to exercise?
Answer: It's very difficult, I acknowledge that. But you know how you don't have to negotiate with yourself about brushing your teeth? You need to get exercise into the same part of your head, so it's not a thing you think about not doing. You just do it because it's what you do. That sounds simple, but it isn't. We would all rather stay in bed or go to the pub, but I suggest you nip that thought in the bud as soon as it pops up. Eventually you'll establish a routine and you'll get good at not having that internal debate. I've been doing this for forty years now and it's second nature. In fact I have to schedule in rest days because I'd just start exercising (for me that means rowing) without thinking otherwise.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What factors contribute to people choosing to live in bad neighborhoods or raise their families there? Are they aware of the potential dangers in these areas?
Answer: I raised my family in Luton, UK. It's a blue collar town about 35 minutes by train from central London. It's multi ethnic with big Asian and Irish communities. It has terrible traffic and was home to the UK's first Arndale Centre, a kind of shitty shopping centre, or rather what 1960's town planners imagined the future of shopping to be. It hosts London's crappiest airport, the one whose new car park recently burnt to the ground. I wouldn't necessarily call it a 'bad neighbourhood', but it's not smart or classy. No one aspires to live there, put it that way. So why did we move there, I hear you ask? Well, I didn't want to, but my wife fell in love with an amazing but run-down old house (in admittedly Luton's best, or least bad area) and would brook no argument. The timing was bad as our oldest son was approaching the age where schools are important and where you live impacts on that. I wasn't keen on any of the Luton schools tbh. But there were advantages too. The house was a steal and it was vast. We would never run out of space. It had a huge and beautiful garden. The commute to work for me was simple and fast. It was close to Harpenden where we were moving from, and we could easily orientate ourselves in that direction. Things worked out ok. The house was renovated. The kids got into a great school in Harpenden, the lovely, leafy small town nearby. All their friends were great and they are close to some of them now, a decade or two later. I commuted to work in central London for years and when I no longer needed to, I had plenty of room to work from home. So did my wife. When we considered that house I remember discussions we had about it and the risks involved. I wouldn't describe them as 'dangers' though. We were never burgled and although we had one noisy neighbour once, I got that sorted out quite quickly. So the 'dangers' were hypothetical, potential. I don't think we really worried about being physically attacked or anything, and in the 16 years we were there, it didn't ever happen. Luton is still not a place I would choose to visit unless I need to get a new tyre, but I look back on that house (which I grew to like rather than love) with great happiness. Shame it had to be there, but if it had been anywhere else, we couldn't have afforded it. We had some of the best years of our lives there.

Name: Nick Schön

Question: Is Germany the best country in Europe, in terms of everything?

Question: What was your biggest culture shock going to Europe?
Answer: I was born in the U.K. and first went to continental Europe with my parents and older brother when I was six or seven, so in the early 1960's. We went to Paris, and I thought it smelled very foreign. I was aware of a sort of sour smell that came from the strong cigarettes seemingly everyone smoked, but there was more. In that whiff was garlic and … Ah yes, urine. My brother and I thought the "pissoires" of Paris were both fascinating (in the way that roadkill is fascinating to young children) but also hilarious. Our parents allowed us to use the ones that were suitable for kids (there were various designs) and that was pretty much the highlight of the trip for us. I am sure our parents were disappointed. These pissoires are now long gone sadly, although someone will no doubt correct me on that. But even now, I can remember the delight of turning that galvanised metal dark with a stream of wee, jiggling with my giggles.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How did the Germans justify their actions during World War II? Did any of them feel guilty or remorseful for their actions?
Answer: The Nazis cast Germans as victims. According to them, everyone was out to do the Germans down and to deprive them of their true destiny. So when the victorious French army occupied the Ruhr industrial region after WW1, it was used to support this argument. The post WW1 years had been extremely hard on Germans, and many looked around for scapegoats. The Nazis were happy to provide them in the form of the Jews. Add to this a weird, dystopian view of race and eugenics, and you have a very toxic mix that basically resulted in the inescapable logic of Nazi aggression being completely justified. They were simply claiming what was rightfully theirs, according to this argument. So when people were encouraged to grass on their neighbour or to reveal where Jews were hiding, in the world they created these acts of cruelty were seen as virtuous. Like George Orwell wrote in 1984, bad became good. It wasn't until 1945 that Germany as a whole was freed from this mad mind-set. The danger facing Europe now is that with the rise of the far right in many countries, the lessons of the past may have to re-learned.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why do some people celebrate religious holidays even if they do not believe in God or any other deity? Is it solely for the purpose of partying or are there other reasons?
