Name: Nick Schön
Question: Was Germany aware of the D-day invasion before it happened? If so, why did they not take any action to prevent or delay it?
Answer: Germany knew that a new front was going to open but they didn't know where or when the landings would be. The Allies went to great trouble to hide preparations and to deceive the Germans into thinking the landings wouldn't happen where they did in fact take place. As a result the Germans had to construct the "Atlantic Wall", a vast stretch of fortifications the length of the French coast. It cost many millions and kept a vast resource of men and materiel from being used elsewhere. The weather in early June 1944 wasn't good. The Germans assumed the Allies wouldn't try a seaborne landing in anything but perfect conditions, and Rommel, who was in charge of coastal defence was so complacent in this decision that he left his post to attend his wife's birthday celebrations in Germany at the crucial time. So successful were the deceptions and so complete was the surprise, that the Germans refused to believe the landings were the main event well after the first day, when beach heads had been secured. The success of D-Day was partly due to a triumph of intelligence but also aided by German complacency.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Can American tourists legally fly a German flag in Germany?
Answer: What is it with the American obsession with flags? No one else cares unless it's offensive. Flap a German flag in Germany and people will just think you're a nationalist idiot. No one will care if you're a confused American.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it culturally acceptable for Germans to view monuments honoring soldiers who fought for Germany during World War II?
Answer: No it isn't and that's why they don't. Even the Nazis didn't erect statues in public much. I suppose they were too busy invading and what not. However this is an interesting question insofar as statues to historical figures (such as Edward Colston) who are now seen in an unfavourable light are frequently themselves controversial. Should they be removed because we now feel they do not deserve to be respected and immortalised with a statue? Should the stature remain, because they did some good works and held values common in their day? Is there a middle path, such as removing the statues to a statue park, or leaving them in place but adding plaques to fully make clear their deeds and misdeeds? The protestors who threw Edward Colston's statue into the river held firm views on this, but those who believe the statue should remain might well hesitate to apply that logic to a statue to Goebbels or Goering, were there to be such things in Germany. There is another way to look at this issue, and that is to see the figures, both good and bad, as part of the national story. So a statue to Ronnie Biggs, the Great Train Robber? Jack the Ripper? Jimmy Saville? If we are going to be brutally honest, maybe. I think Germans are more brutally honest about their past than the British are. If you disagree, can you imagine Thatcher kneeling before a monument to the Boers in South Africa?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why in the UK, do we allow so many young men, arriving illegally, allegedly fleeing war? If our grandparents had said, "no, I'm not fighting the Germans in WWII, I'm off to Australia etc", without these brave boys, it would be v different
Answer: Britain actually has a long tradition of helping refugees fleeing persecution and seeking sanctuary. My father was a refugee as was his brother, who was old enough to enlist in the British 8th Army and fight in his Cromwell tank until the war ended. "These brave boys" in fact includes many who Britain would now seek to return to their tormentors.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why do some people refuse to use self checkout lanes in stores?
Answer: The Tesco self checkouts are easily the worst I've ever used. They never work and always require an employee to reset them. M&S' aren't much better. Waitrose give you a hand scanner to use as you roam the shop and that never fails. By far the best system.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: For metro and suburban rail journeys from Central London to various M25 towns in several different directions, is it true that for large swathes of many such journeys you may not hear passengers speaking ENGLISH? Are other UK cities becoming similar?
Answer: So what? I mean, what is the actual problem here? People speaking a language offends other people? Well boo hoo. It’s a free country and they shouldn’t be eavesdropping anyway. They should mind their own business. London is very fortunate in that it’s home to many different foreign communities, all of whom also speak English since the Brits are famously monoglot. Critics are basically moaning about people who are better educated and have more language ability than they do precisely because the latter are more skilled. The Reform party are in favour of some skilled immigration, so if even these mini-fascists can tolerate Portuguese or Hindi on the train, surely everyone can too.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is the reason for German using different words for 'to eat' and 'to drink' compared to English?
Answer: English uses two words for these actions, and they are both related to the German “essen” and “trinken”. However there is one significant difference: in German you’d never say an animal “eats”. German uses “Fressen” to describe an animal eating, whereas there is no such distinction other than the slang “scoff” in English.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Britain. A total of 430,104 shoplifting offences were recorded by police in 2023 and that is just the ones reported. Film of 3 black men laughing as they steal from a shop, knowing the police will do nothing. Are the police no longer fit for purpose?
Answer: Perhaps the money so eagerly handed to Rwanda for accommodation that will never be used should be channeled towards making the U.K. a better place to live in. Criminalising a whole category of people who only want a good life seems an odd thing to do when there are some already here who are determined to live a bad one.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How does tea improve your mood?
Answer: Everyone has some food or drink that gives them comfort. It might be something from their childhood that reminds them of their grandma or grandpa, or a sweet they associate with a holiday or happy event. That's why foodstuffs we never eat at other times and which aren't even liked all that much are still prepared. I'm thinking Christmas pudding for example. It's a very heavy, sweet, fruity dessert that is eaten at no other time. I have a Scottish friend who lives in Brussels, and when I visit him I have to bring some Lucozade because he can't get it there and it instantly reminds him of his mother comforting him when he was ill in bed as a child. (It was marketed as a drink to have when you're ill, long before it was associated with sport). Tea is a bit like that for me. It reminds me of happy, peaceful, rainy afternoons spent drawing, painting and making things at home as a child. It's instant comfort. It's calming. Before having an afternoon nap (an increasingly frequent occurrence) I often have a mug of Yorkshire tea with milk. The narcotic effect of the comfort it gives far outweighs the chemical stimulation of the caffeine and it's nap o'clock in minutes. It's impossible to be in a bad mood after that.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Can you provide some examples of atheists who do not fit the typical stereotype?
Answer: The only thing that's stereotypical of atheists is their disbelief in a god. I'm struggling to think of what else there is.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Will Reform UK leader Nigel Farage win a Parliamentary seat in Clacron?
Answer: This is of course up to the people of Clacton. Farage has is followers just as Trump has his, and like them, Farage is something of a cult. That cult following has been insufficient in the past to get him elected…seven times in fact, and I sincerely hope it becomes eight, but who knows? It’s up to whoever is ahead in the polls in that constituency at the moment to make sure they stay ahead. I would recommend tactical voting to keep the nasty little blackshirt-in-tweeds out.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do you find yourself thinking about work even when you are supposed to be enjoying leisure activities?
Answer: As an advertising creative, I often carried on thinking about a problem on my way home. During the evening, there it was, ticking away in the background. Part of my mind must have been trying to solve the loose end the problem had become. I kept a pen and paper by my bed because I found the relaxed state I entered before sleep was particularly likely to generate good ideas. I don’t want to give the impression that this was conscious or forced. I wasn’t distracted. The whole idea of creative idea generation is that it is essentially playful, and so even when you’re doing something quite unrelated and fully focussed on it, a thought or idea can pop up out of that app you have running in your head in the background. I found it fruitful and enjoyable even.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What can you practice with a degree in religion?
Answer: A degree is often not intended to train you for a particular job. If that were the case we'd be awash with English and History experts equipped only to teach. A degree often just teaches you to think. I knew a history graduate who got a job as a brand manager for Proctor & Gamble. He didn't study Shampoo at uni, or get a degree in Marketing. He had studied Ancient History and had used it to develop thinking skills P&G prized. So a degree in Theology might develop your mind so that Law is very attractive to you and a small step to make. In fact a cousin did exactly that and is now a Barrister.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are some reasons why atheists do not believe in God? Is it due to intelligence or lack of education on the subject?
Answer: No one tampered with my innate common sense when I was a child.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do all atheists believe that all religions are wrong, or do they have specific beliefs about certain religions? What are the reasons behind their beliefs?
Answer: Atheists just disbelieve. Some are against religious belief everywhere too, some just aren't enthusiastic about religion per se, some are kind of ok with one religion but are vehemently anti all the others, some absolutely hate one particular religion because of personal experience and just passively disbelieve all others, and some are quite happy to disbelieve and let others do whatever they want in the mysticism zone. There are lots of other variations too I'm sure, but as a general rule atheists is a very loose term to describe someone who simply does not believe in any god. Another way of putting it is: imagine all the gods there are that you disbelieve in. An atheist and you are perfectly aligned. They just disbelieve in one more.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Isn’t dragging a former President, who is running for President again, through criminal courts over something so trivial, clearly a political move to ruin his image and make it harder for him to become president?
Answer: Surely the law has to be applied equally? I mean, if it was suspected that Joe Biden had paid a porn star to keep quiet and put it through his company as a business expense, I bet Republicans wouldn't give him a free pass because it was, you know, "so trivial". The law applies to us all. Fairness and equality in the eyes of the law is the cornerstone of a civilised country. Or are you suggesting that the USA isn't in that category?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How is nationality decided for people who hold multiple nationalities/passports, especially when they are travelling outside said countries? Do they get to declare whatever nationality they feel like?
Answer: Yeah, you can pretty much use whichever passport is best for the job, depending on the country you're entering or leaving and the nationality of your passports. Just pick the most appropriate one, or if both seem appropriate, the one that gets you into the shortest queue.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it possible to leave a country using someone else's passport?
Answer: Apparently so. A few years ago I caught a Eurostar train to Brussels from London. It wasn't until I had gone through passport control and was on the train that I realised I had picked up my father's Austrian passport instead of mine. It had been looked at but no one noticed that it had expired, that he looked quite unlike me, was twenty years older than me and was dead. I used my British passport for the rest of the trip.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: If there were only 30 countries in the world, which ones should remain and why?
Answer: I'd like to book one slot for Switzerland. Beautiful, peaceful, safe, respectful, doesn't interfere with others, makes multiculturalism work, rich, lovely climate, lovely chocolate. Not saying it's perfect (giving women the vote only recently?), but pretty nice compared to N.Korea. Nice native music even.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How can you persuade your husband to invest in stocks instead of real estate?
Answer: Show him the calculations. I've just done them and have decided to get out of property. The returns have been poor for some time now. Even though rents have gone up, so have costs and there's been no capital growth lately. The spreadsheet does not lie. The latest straw for my camel's back was a new property license I have to get in order to rent out a property in London. I have to pay £800 for permission to be a landlord. That made me think "Hang on a second…" I calculated that I could sell up, take a lump sum out for whatever, and still achieve the same returns by investing in bonds. The independent financial advisor I contacted said a lot of private landlords are doing the same.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: As a Korean descendant, I am boycotting Japanese products due to their cruelty to my ancestors. By that same logic, should Jews boycott German products due to the Nazis' actions?
Answer: Possibly, but these events were a long time ago now and the perpetrators are all dead. Exactly who is benefitting from this boycott? Having said that, go ahead. It's your money. My mother didn't like the idea of owning a German car because she was an adult in wartime London and was bombed out. She wasn't Jewish, but just chose not to buy German stuff. In time her position softened and she even owned an Audi Coupé, but it was her choice.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is Diane Abbot an asset or liability to the Labour Party's 2024 general election campaign?
Answer: She is an asset to her constituents who seem to like her. She is also an asset to the Labour Party as she is a woman of colour, and very intelligent too. Less of an asset is her politics. She is considered a left wing Corbynite, and that is a big turn-off for many wavering voters. So I'd say Starmer is right to readmit her to Labour (her punishment seemed pretty harsh in the first place) and right to let her run. She will win her seat, so big tick there. But he won't let her near the cabinet and will withdraw the whip straight away if she speaks out of turn.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Have any atheists considered converting to a religion but ultimately decided against it? What factors influenced their decision and what could potentially change their mind in the future?
Answer: You make a deeply held belief sound like a decision to buy a tent. I don't think a religious conviction works like that. At least it shouldn't.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How does the German government know whether someone is using the swastika as a Nazi or religious symbol?
Answer: In Germany any possible connection with religion was smothered by its political meaning many decades ago. It is an incredibly loaded and meaningful symbol. The swastika was at one time a symbol of luck. Not now. It has been described as 'symbol of the century' because it communicates so powerfully. It is impossible to see it as anything other than standing for Nazism. That is why it is banned except for educational purposes.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Have you ever worked at a company where there is constant drama and cussing?
Answer: I worked in advertising in the '70's, 80's, 90's and 00's, and yes, absolutely…in fact the "dramas and cussing" was the least of it. There was a regular smell of weed in the creative dept, plenty of coke and one agency I worked at for 15 years even had its own pub, so getting plastered was kind of company policy. There were fist fights. One member of staff was involved in the big Harrods safety deposit box hold-up. In fact there was all manner of appalling behaviour. It was glorious.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do you identify as a corporate person?
Answer: I tried it and tbh, it wasn't me. I was pretty proud of my first office…air conditioned in Frankfurt with a view over the city. I didn't really care much about the advertising agencies I worked for beyond the opportunities they gave me to do good creative work. The corporate body itself? That was way above my pay grade. I was employed to do a specific creative job, and I knew that if I didn't do a good job they would drop me. So singing the company song was an irrelevancy. When I went freelance I felt very liberated. I could go to an ad agency, come up with some ideas or maybe do a pitch for some new biz and then just walk away. The pay was better and I didn't have to get involved in office politics. When I then became an illustrator I realised that not even having to go into those offices was an enjoyment in itself.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Have you ever bought something specifically because you saw it in a movie or TV show?
Answer: Personally no, but a friend fell in love with Steve McQueen's '68 Mustang Fastback in "Bullitt" and years later when he had the money, bought one. It wasn't in Forest Green, but it is rather gorgeous when the restoration was done.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Would you consider working for a company that allows you to have a side hustle?
Answer: I did, for quite a few years. I was working for an advertising agency (as a creative) by day and working on children's books as an illustrator by night. The agency didn't mind. In fact other art directors in my agency sometimes commissioned me to illustrate ads for them and I got paid extra for doing it. It was great. In time the illustration work grew so I went freelance as an advertising creative and had more time for drawing and painting. Eventually it took over completely and I gave up advertising.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What would you do if a friend met you suddenly after a long time?
Answer: It depends why you stopped seeing one another. I had a close schoolmate. We drifted apart when I graduated and moved abroad although I kept up with other school friends I wasn't so close to. We met again thirty years later at a school reunion, and straight away I realised why our friendship withered. He was entirely focussed on himself and wasn't at all curious about me or my wife (who he had also known when we were at school). I mentioned this to some friends from our circle. Quite independently they came to the same conclusion. No one kept up with him, which was a shame. We had him and his wife over for supper and I called him once later. There was no reciprocation and I assumed that he was indifferent. It wasn't personal. He didn't bother with any of our circle from school. I tried.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Can you give examples of foods that do not look like their actual taste? How do these foods differ from each other?
Answer: We once had an Icelandic friend over for breakfast. He was talking away and slathering his toast with Marmite. Still in full flow, he took a bite and shot out of his chair. "What…the…fuck…is…this?" he spluttered. He assumed it was Nutella or some chocolate spread, and I can see how he might have thought that by looking at it. Marmite is very much part of the British culture. Although there is a similar product in Australia (Vegemite) it's pretty unique, as is the advertising for it. Here's a brilliant recent example.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Which country is known for making the best cakes, fine pastries, and desserts in terms of taste: Germany or France? Why?
Answer: Both make excellent pastries and cakes, but neither can equal Austria.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Have you ever purchased something that came from watching a television or streaming ad?
Answer: Kind of, although it was me who made the ad. I was working for the advertising agency who had the Head & Shoulders account. My work on it meant that I learned a lot about how thorough Proctor & Gamble are and how good it actually is. I learned that P&G are actually pretty determined not to claim things that their products can't deliver, and when I used H&S myself, i noticed I didn't get dandruff. So when my free samples ran out, I started buying it myself. I must have made four or five TV commercials for them…more probably. We even flew to Albuquerque from London to shoot one once (it's a long story), and they were all enjoyable and successful. Later I worked on Pantene, which really does deliver shiny hair as it claims, if that's your thing. I tried it too, but went back to H&S, because you never get a second chance to make a first impression.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is your favourite German lager?
Answer: I know it's considered pretty average but there's a special place in my heart for Dortmunder Union.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Which countries consume more sausage than Germany? Why do they not consume it as frequently as Germans? Are there any other countries with unique types of sausages that differ from German sausages?
Answer: I bet they eat more sausage in Poland. The Poles are know almost live on them.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is something you‘ve seen in another country & you wish to be in yours too?
Answer: I've been swimming in lakes in Austria for years. They are spotless. The water is like bottled water. Boats are permitted, but not motor boats…only sailing or electric boats. Nothing is allowed in the water that could pollute it. Contrast this with the sewage-filled rivers and lakes in the U.K.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are the circumstances in which you would flee your home and leave behind your artwork?
Answer: My artwork is a bit of a liability tbh. I have boxes of it, but since I have it all digitised and stored in a cloud, it's not really a problem if it all went up in flames. I'd leave it all behind in a case of fire, flood, alien/zombie invasion without a second thought.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What do you think are the key reasons why the Conservative Party has been in power for so long?
Answer: The Tories have been in power for so long because for most of that time the opposition has been unviable. Jeremy Corbyn rendered the Labour Party unelectable. Now they have a serious, left of centre leader, guess what's going to happen (bar some unforeseen calamity)?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Can you give some examples of behaviors that are considered rude in other countries but not in Germany?
Answer: Walking into a mixed public sauna stark naked. No German would turn a hair, in fact it is expected, but it would cause some serious arm waving in Italy, some serious tutting in England and in America people would start screaming and fainting.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Nigel Farage says that “I can't imagine we've ever had two leaders going head to head for who's going to be the next prime minister, who are, frankly, so boring… we can predict a very, very low turnout”. Will Farage be correct about the low turnout?
Answer: Dunno, but when you think about it, why is it important for a politician to be exciting? I want my politicians to be honest, moral and have good judgement, like Attlee for instance. He was famously dull, but he was a far, far better PM than say Boris Johnson, who passed up no opportunity to brazenly spotlight himself. By saying this, Farage reveals what a vacuous waste of space he is. He thinks politicians have to behave like contestants on telly. I think you don't get institutions like the NHS by having a silly hair-do. You need serious political heft, and I think the British voters are fed up with Tory air-heads.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: With reports of the UK's Conservative Party trying to bring back mandatory national service are the Tories trying to lose in a landslide in the next election?
Answer: No, they are resigned to losing. But they think they can at least do this with some dignity. By appealing to right-wing voters who might pick Reform, they hope to at least not be totally humiliated. This ill thought out policy of National Service is absurd. No one apart from aged armchair generals and cantankerous old curmudgeons think it has any merit. The armed forces certainly wouldn't know what to do with a huge influx of reluctant conscripts. The Tories have revealed that they are fighting to come second and fear having the right-wing mantle stolen from them. They are desperate.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Now this might be a bit hard for a lot of liberals to understand, but do you know you can be right-wing and not a Nazi?
Answer: Of course. Most of my Jewish friends are quite right of centre by my reckoning. I expect most will vote Tory at the next election, even though the likes of Suella Braverman would have fought to send their parents and grandparents back to Central Europe to await their fates. All Nazis are right wing but not all right wingers are Nazis.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it legal to sell something that has no value?
Answer: If someone s prepared to pay something for it, then that is its value to them. "Value" is not something you can really define otherwise. You can say "it cost me this much to make" but that doesn't mean it's worth that much (or ideally more) to someone else. Manufactures go to great lengths to convince us that their product is fantastic. Sometimes we allow ourselves to believe it at least in part, and buy it. Rarely does the value we put on it bear a close relation to the actual cost of making it though. They have to make a profit or there's no reason for them to do it. I hear that in some parts of the world women sell their used underwear. As distasteful as this may seem, it bears out what I think. People have differing definitions of what is of value, and in that difference there is profit to be made.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Should women give men haircuts?
Answer: Not if they are bad at it. My late wife once tried cutting my hair and she made a real pigs ear of it. It was hilarious. I went to a barber straight away and he asked me if my wife was blind.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: I sent my tenant a 90-day notice that I will not renew his lease, he said he will sue for retaliation. Can I counter sue for him being a hostile tenant?
Answer: Calm down and drop all the lawyer nonsense. You've given your tenant what here in the UK is considered adequate notice. It's perfectly fair and legal. No one has to get excited about this unless the tenant doesn't move out. There is a perfectly normal protocol for what happens after this.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do atheists ever consider converting to a religion due to the peaceful and welcoming atmosphere of many churches?
Answer: Some churches are nice places, and I've yet to meet a Christian that hasn't meant me well. Some of my best friends have a strong religious faith and derive much strength and support from the community they belong to. But here's the thing: I just don't believe in a god…any god. I completely understand the benefits of being in a community of like minded people, but in the same way that I don't get to enjoy the benefits of being in a golf club because I'm not interested in golf, I can never get to enjoy the benefits of being a Christian, Jew or whatever because I'm just not interested in their belief and never have been. Like nearly everyone I know, I have communities or circles of friends and pursue activities perfectly adequately without any religious element to my life. I don't think there would be any genuine benefit for anyone to become involved with a religious community just for the "peaceful and welcoming atmosphere of many churches", which lets face it, are open to the non-believing members of the public too most of the time anyway.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why do doctors ask if you smoke? Is it solely for insurance purposes or are there other reasons for this question?
Answer: My doctor asked me if I smoke when we first met, and I live in the UK where we have universal healthcare, so no insurance in the sense that Americans understand the term. I believe he asked me this to determine what to look out for with me. Smoking impacts on so many aspects of health and it's a big factor in many serious illnesses, so he probably would have thought "Hmmm…he's complaining about a persistent cough and he's been smoking for decades…that could be just a smokers cough or maybe something more serious…", whereas as I've never smoked, he might just think "Hmmm…he probably just needs some antibiotics to shake this off". I'm in my late 60's, so it's about time for a life of puffing to make its presence felt. I'd be more prone to heart and lung disease for starters. He'd want to check that and all the other possibilities too.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How do atheists explain the fact that some church hymns, like How Great Thou Art and Lord I Lift Your Name on High, are so beautiful? Doesn't that point to some sort of divine inspiration?
Answer: Some hymns are tuneful, but precious few. Many are just tired dirges with unintelligible, dreadful lyrics. If that's the best your god can do by way of inspiration, I'm unimpressed. Having said that, his architecture is impressive.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why do people spend millions of dollars to buy a shoebox condo in an overpriced big city when they could spend half that much with twice the space in a cheaper less congested area?
Answer: Some people really like big cities. I do too. I like the buzz, the variety, the atmosphere and the food. I like the anonymity. For people like that, maybe the location, location, location is the driving force behind what they wish to buy, as opposed to mere square metres.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why is it that people in countries who have universal healthcare who don't mind the free rider problem, assume that everybody else should also just ignore the free rider problem?
Answer: Is that an issue for other things the state provides? Do you think that no one should be protected by the armed forces because there might be some tax dodgers who haven't paid their share getting protected? And what about roads? All those free riders who just ride bicycles and pay no road tax. Rip up the roads, surely. Or schools? All those poor people on benefits, having the temerity to educate their children! What a nerve! Far better to shut down all the schools to stop the free rider problem, no?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are the reasons behind UKIP's lack of success in local elections and overall?
Answer: There is no one constituency where all the extreme right wingers live. They are sprinkled throughout the country, so it's fortunately hard for them to dominate any one area.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What were the reasons for the high number of German U-boat sinkings during World War II? Was it due to poor quality or operation?
Answer: U-boats were incredibly dangerous to the Allies. They posed an existential threat to the U.K., so every stop was pulled out to avoid them and sink them. In the end, these measures were pretty successful but not every U-boat was sunk.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: If the 6 million Jews who died in the Holocaust are still paid by Germany today, why is England not paying black African people for slavery?
Answer: The descendants of perpetrators of the Holocaust have a different attitude to the wrongs of their recent past to that of the English and the wrongs of their much more distant past. Germany and Austria still pay victims of National Socialism. If my father was still alive, he would still be receiving money from Austria. As his son, they have made an exception and granted me and those like me dual nationality. I don't think this goes anywhere near atonement or compensation, but it is at least an acknowledgment that wrongs were committed by the state and that's something. It was late but at least arrived. I think better of Austria now they have adopted this policy. I see modern Austrians as a lot different to those of one or two generations ago. I expect Austrians feel better too. I think it is better to acknowledge mistakes than to make excuses or to double down on them. Times have changed and it does Britain no good to align itself with the past by not formally making the difference quite clear. Britain makes much of its attachment to the past. Not even apologising for the transparent wrongs is inexcusable.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How do people who don't have a steady income afford expensive clothes? How can you determine if expensive clothes are fake or not?
Answer: I know a few well-dressed people who buy used ("pre-loved") clothes online or from good charity shops in nice areas. There was a shop like that in Hampstead, London. It had some wonderful stock at good prices. They were very, very picky about what they would accept…I know because my late wife used to sell her unwanted designer things there sometimes. She had friends who went there to buy and sometimes she would take something in and return with something else.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Where can I buy a used car in Germany?
Answer: I bought one used from a VW dealer, one from a friend, one from an ad, one from a guy who was a friend of a friend and one new one from the advertising agency I worked for. We had the Ford account and I got a big discount. Didn't really want a Ford but it was too good to pass up.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is considered an excessive amount of money to spend on restoring an old classic car?
Answer: £1 more than it's worth when finished. Actually that's not entirely true, because it's quite possible to have a sentimental affection to a particular model and if that's the case, common sense flies out of the window and the only thing that stops you is bankruptcy or imminent divorce.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What’s the most important reason that you’ll never visit certain countries again?
Answer: I will probably never go to Nigeria again. Nigerians are lovely people. I've been to Nigeria many times and have never had a bad experience. However that may be because Jason, with his AK-47 never left my side. He wasn't there because I requested him to be. Our client who was Nigerian, simply arranged Jason as a matter of course. Nigeria is a big country and has some beauty spots, but Lagos, where I spent most of my time, isn't one of them. To be blunt, it's a crowded jumble of ruins and part constructed buildings with a few nice compounds. It's also got a bit of a problem with rubbish, insofar as it's everywhere. I don't know how often it's collected, but my guess is seldom. The world is full of lovely places, and that's why I won't be rushing back to Nigeria. There's only a finite amount of time available. Sorry.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do you think it's important to have a handheld fan while traveling during summer, as recommended by shopping editors?
Answer: Depends on where you are. I'm in the U.K. and a handheld umbrella is far more important.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How long can you stay in a country as a tourist?
Answer: I notice this a lot… the assumption that there is some sort of world government that decides universal rules. There isn't. The world is pretty chaotic, and that is why each country makes its own rules regarding how long tourists can stay.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it common for elderly individuals to become angry and bitter? Are there any effective ways to address this issue besides giving them space?
Answer: Well it's certainly true that getting old has its challenges. Diminishing capacity, diminishing health, a general sense of decline and that the best is in the past…all reasons to be a bit miserable. Add to that the loss of beloved family and friends and often reduced income, and you have a scenario that isn't necessarily optimistic. But. Not all older people see this as their lives even if some of these elements exist for them. Many have purpose, family and friends they love, hobbies and activities. However if the former is the situation, abandoning them is unlikely to make them any happier. It might be a big ask, but doing the opposite and spending time with them doing things they like, might be the correct course.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it weird to not want to visit Europe if you don't find European civilization to be fascinating?
Answer: No, it's perfectly ok to not be interested in something a lot of other people like. Be your authentic you. We have a limited time on earth and I see no benefit in spending the small portion of it allotted to holidays visiting things you aren't interested in. Having said that, I am very much for trying new things and not staying in my comfort zone. That's how we all learn and grow.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How can one cope with negative experiences while traveling abroad? Is the effort of traveling worth it if it is not enjoyable?
Answer: We've all had disappointments. The theft. The horrible meal. The rude shop assistant. The delayed flight. Not all were actually disasters though, so let's not over-dramatise things. The way I deal with it is to learn from the incident but to travel more. So because I had a horrible experience skiing in France, I still ski, but I go to Austria. I have kind of done Milan where I was ripped off so simply don't need to go there again…etc, etc. I focus on what I like and what has been successful, and do more of that, and I try not to repeat mistakes. But I try to keep it in perspective…one rude Parisian isn't going to ruin France for me. Later this year I'm driving a 1967 Mustang Fastback from London to Vienna. My route is going to take in places I love in France, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland and Austria, places I've always wanted to see, and I'm sure there will be one or two incidents that don't work out too well. That will be all part of the adventure.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are some reasons why people may not enjoy visiting Italy compared to other European countries like France and Germany?
Answer: I was there last summer and it was quite hot and the cities were crowded with tourists like me. Not everyone thinks that combo is pleasant. Germany isn't such a tourist destination for the international traveller, although Berlin is firmly on that particular map. France has its hot, crowded towns but they are in the south. Away from the Mediterranean coast and towns like Biarritz on the Atlantic side, many French towns are fairly quiet in the summer.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is your family's approach to spending money on vacations to Europe? How do you decide on which places to visit?
Answer: Before I was an adult, it was up to my parents. They chose the destinations and handled the budgets. As the family prospered we progressed from camping to some good hotels. As I grew and became more adult I chose where to go. My first foreign holiday was after my exams when I was 17. A friend had a Ford and four of us drove from our homes in London to the south of France. We camped and youth hostelled because we had a tiny budget, but it was glorious. I have always travelled in Europe for the last 7 years. I decide where to go based on who and what I want to see and experience. Europe is fascinating, varied and exciting.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why do we often pay more for things than their actual production cost, especially for luxury items?
Answer: The maker has to make a profit and there are distribution and marketing costs too of course. Add to that, the brand has a value. The badge of a Ferrari for instance is worth a lot to some people. All brands mean something and carry a baggage they carefully curate to appeal to their customers. Get it right, and it adds a lot to the perceived value of the actual product.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is it wrong of me to lie down in bed when I pray to God at night, or must I be on my knees?
Answer: Surely a simple experiment will answer your question. One method will work and the other won't.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why do people from developed countries allow assisted suicide?
Answer: Because people want the option to end their lives on their terms. In a sense it's the ultimate human right. People end their lives all the time. It's always sad and mostly it's avoidable. The lonely divorcee who drinks herself to death, the bankrupt who hangs himself, etc. These people are depressed and need help that is often unavailable. In countries that allow assisted dying, they'd be weeded out. The bar is set quite high and they don't just bump off anyone who walks in off the street. The purpose of assisted dying is to allow those who have a genuine and verified medical condition that is unbearable to take control over how long their suffering (and that of those they love) goes on for. I think it's brave and honourable and if I find myself in that position, I'll do it.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Can an estate agent be friends with a landlord?
Answer: Of course, but as a landlord I prefer to keep my dealings with estate agents professional. There is a difference between being friendly and being friends.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Would a landlord tax solve the housing problem?
Answer: I'm a landlord, and if a tax was levied so that it wasn't profitable for me to have property for rent any more, I'd sell. The properties would be probably bought by owner-occupiers, so that would mean fewer properties to rent. Multiply this many times over and it will mean property prices fall a little because there are more on the market, but there will be fewer to rent. So rents will go up. I don't see how this solves the housing crisis.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Would Labour still be cruising to a (probable) electoral victory if they were still led by Jeremy Corbyn?
Answer: Probably not. Corbyn scared the shit out of middle England and was a really easy target for Tories, determined to cast Labour as a radical hard-left, dogma-driven cult. Experience shows that voters like middle of the road politicians and Corbyn wasn't that. Even with this right-wing, failed and desperate Tory Party he probably wouldn't have seemed like a better choice to a lot of people. Starmer may not be perfect but he is a centrist safe pair of hands leading a party which isn't old, exhausted and as contaminated as a glass of Devon tap water.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: At what point, if ever, did British troops, sailors and airmen come to believe that they were fighting a monstrous evil in WW2, rather than defending the British Empire?
Answer: My uncle Hugh, on the left, was a tanker in a Cromwell tank. He was also a Jewish Austrian refugee who got to London in 1938 with my Dad, his little brother. He had no doubt about the evil he was fighting. In fact that is why he volunteered to fight his countrymen, even though it might not have been pleasant had he been captured. He didn't disguise his heritage although he anglicised his first name. He really wasn't interested in the British Empire. in fact I doubt if he approved of it. He survived some brutal combat and married the prettiest girl in Hamburg.

Question: What are the benefits of paying rent on time for tenants?
Answer: I think a tenant that always pays on time is a "good tenant" that I want to keep, so at the renewal time I'm much more likely to cut them a deal.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What should a landlord say to a tenant who repeatedly has excuses for not paying their rent despite working full time and being flush?
Answer: I have been in that situation and I handled it badly by accepting their excuses. It cost me thousands in the end. So now I would tell the tenant that they obviously couldn't afford to rent my place and serve the section (I think it's 21 but that might be out of date) to move out.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How long after death does it take for the spirit to leave the body?
Answer: There are anecdotal stories from people of a religious persuasion of souls leaving a body. However I am yet to be persuaded that this has ever been recorded, let alone scientifically verified. Furthermore, there is no evidence that there is a soul at all. That doesn't mean it's not true. Science doesn't know everything by any means. But there is simply no evidence that it might be true even. I mean, we suspected that the Higgs-Boson particle existed based on a theory. An experiment was designed and indeed it was proved to exist. That has simply not been the case with souls. There is no evidence, no suspicion by eminent scientists, no test. What there is are people who claim to see a light (usually). But here's the thing: people with a strong religious belief at a time of stress are liable to see stuff. Witnesses to crime (religious or otherwise) often imagine they see things that they cannot possibly have seen, and not seen things that were right in front of them. Humans are pretty unreliable. I know it's comforting to believe in an afterlife. I really wish I did. But I simply don't buy it, any more than I believe in any other magical story that makes us feel better about something awful and hard to accept like the loss of a loved one.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Do hotels have to tell you if someone has ever died in the room you rent?
Answer: No. But I have other news for you. Probably in every house (bar new ones) you've been in, people have died. At this minute you're probably not very far from human remains even. For millennia people have been dying all over the place, every day. It's part of life. It's perfectly normal.

Question: If you were a landlord and you owned a lot of property and one of your best friends came to you and asked if they can rent one of your places but you knew that this person wasn't trustworthy when it came to rent would you rent to them anyway?

Question: Would you buy a product just because a TV or any famous person advertised the product?
Answer: Not just because they endorse it, no, but it makes a difference if I was going to buy something in that product category anyway. Take coffee machines. I like George Clooney and identify a bit with him, so when he recommended Nespresso I thought I'd consider that brand as I was in the market for a new coffee machine. I ended up with a Nespresso, but closed my account two years later because it's stupidly expensive and they don't seem very good at collecting the empty pods for recycling. So a celebrity endorsement can work on me, but it depends on the celebrity, the product category and the product itself too. It has to deliver what I want and do so consistently, but a celebrity is a good way of attracting my attention in the first place.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Were you popular in high school?
Answer: Yes, but also no. I was popular with a cohort of other boys but I don’t think the school establishment approved. I went to a very academic, private all boys school in the UK. However I didn’t really fit in because I wasn’t interested in sport and not in the top sets in any academic subject. The only thing that changed was that when puberty hit, I lost weight and gained focus. I wasn’t outstanding at anything except art, a subject that was not academic and therefore seen as ‘unworthy’. I was good at English but as I took art seriously, I was an anomaly. This alone made me popular with a group of slightly rebellious boys. (The school was full of factions, the sporty boys, the brainy boys, the Jewish boys, the hopeless boys…often boys were in more than one faction. I seemed to fit in none, except the ones who lived near me who also didn't identify strongly with any other group). I lived near the school and had the run of my house before my mum got home from work at about six, so my friends used to congregate for cigarettes, tea and toast after school. I really think those afternoons with my cohort of friends were the most formative aspect of school for me. They certainly gave me a loyal gaggle, several of whom I still see regularly over 50 years later. We discussed Python, music, cars, motorbikes, irregular French verbs, Shakespeare, Chaucer, Oscar Wilde and Harold Pinter a lot. We were very pretentious. The huge mystery of the opposite gender was endlessly examined, although none of us had a clue what we were taking about. One or two of my friends had sisters…older ones who didn’t acknowledge us and younger ones who were desperate for our attention. I achieved a modicum of fame when at 17, I became the boyfriend of the most stunning girl for miles around. We were a couple, and amazingly, we later married and were very happy until she died. I was quite comfortable being a square peg in a round hole at that school, because I knew I would leave there for art college and I was confident about what I wanted to do after that. About 30% of my year went to Oxbridge and the rest all went to good universities, which sounded as dreary as hell to me. I wanted to mix with common people, as the song goes. I don’t know if I was one of the ‘cool’ boys…I wasn't one of the stellar, bright ones, but I had a car, an empty house, liberal parents and a confidence that served me well in years to come.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Does unhealthy food make you age fast?
Answer: Unhealthy food is often associated with high fat and sugar content. That means you eat a lot of stuff that makes you hungry again sooner, so you tend to put on weight. Being overweight or obese is bad for your health and you'll look and feel bad too. As one ages one generally puts on a bit of weight especially around the middle. Eat fast food, highly processed food and food that's high in carbs and fat and that'll happen sooner.

Question: Is it true that some doctors recommend smoking for health reasons? How much validity is there to this claim?
Answer: What possible "health reason" legitimises a practice that kills millions every year?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What are the most important values you believe are necessary for sustaining a long-term relationship?
Answer: Authenticity. Be yourself, and if that's not what your partner wants, so be it. At least you aren't pretending to be something you aren't. You'll feel much better if you're honest with and true to yourself. Empathy. Understand your partners needs and position. Listen. Put yourself in the position of others, but understand that we aren't all the same. Kindness. Treat every occasion as an opportunity to be nice, even if you aren't met half way. Don't even consider revenge or punishment. Sometimes you'll have to be less than 100% honest in order not to hurt their feelings, but that's ok. Humour. Many tricky situations can be solved if you interpret them with good humour. Not every disaster is a disaster…some become pretty funny in hindsight, so just get to that position sooner. I've never met people in successful long-term relationships that don't laugh a lot both with and at each other and themselves.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Can you provide some examples of advertising objectives and explain why advertisers use them? What does it mean for a campaign to have a clear set of advertising objectives?
Answer: I created this double page newspaper ad for a government body whose function was to convince people in the U.K. to conserve energy. It ran in the Financial Times, the national daily for business. That was the objective of the ad campaign. Get people thinking about saving energy. Incredible as it seems today, in the 1980's this was a new idea to a lot of people. The ad was designed to attract the attention of readers whilst still being legible itself. It was just one ad in a campaign that helped put the whole idea of energy conservation on the map. Without a clear objective, the job of a creative is terribly hard. "Sell more widgets" is an impossible brief. Creatives can only really do their job if a clear task is defined for them. In this era we used briefing forms with an area for the "Single Minded Proposition", and it really did have to be just one single thought. It's what I looked for first. I suspect that has since been superseded by other briefing methods but I'd be surprised if it has produced work that communicates as clearly.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: What is the appropriate age for a man to wear a tuxedo? Can older men still wear a tuxedo and look good?
Answer: The rule of thumb I use is that the more crumpled my body gets, the better my clothes need to be. It therefore follows that a tuxedo has no upper age limit. I think there should be a lower age limit though. Seeing children dressed as mini-adults looks slightly creepy to me, so I suggest a tuxedo should be worn by boys from about 14 or so as the occasion demands. So not to go to the skate park for instance.

Question: Should a father support his adult children indefinitely?
Answer: Support can take many forms. It can mean financial help, and that rather depends on who has what. It can mean time, childcare, anything really…I don't think there is a common rule, so there's no "should", but I think it's usual for any great financial discrepancy between parents and children to be balanced somewhat. The Beatles famously bought their parents houses when they became wealthy for instance, and I'm sure Jeff Bezos' dad gets a nice present every Christmas. I'm equally sure Bill Gates' children are well looked after. The rule, if there is one, is to be nice to people generally, but especially those you love. That means supporting them in any way you can and they want. Picking up your grandchildren from school, running errands, helping out by offering praise, encouragement or a sympathetic ear…these fall under the umbrella of 'support' and are of a type that money can't buy. I believe they should continue indefinitely even if the financial variety can't.

Question: What is the funniest joke you've been told that you still think about to this day?
Answer: A man goes into a pub and orders three pints all at once. He slowly drinks all three, then leaves. He does this every Friday for a month or so, when finally the barman says "Wouldn't it be better if I pour you a pint at a time, so each will be fresh when you come to drink it?" "That's sensible" says the man, half way through the first pint "except I have two brothers, one in Australia and one in Canada and I like to imagine the three of us sitting here having a drink all together" "I see" says the barman, and nothing more is said. Just after Christmas the man comes in and orders just two pints. He looks miserable, and so the barman assumes something has happened to one of the brothers. "I'm so sorry for you loss" he says. "Oh, my brothers are fine" the man says, "It's me…I'm doing dry January".

Question: Would you take a high-speed train ride on the Channel Tunnel over a plane ride?
Answer: Yes, and in fact I did so recently. I was invited to Brussels for a few days, so I worked it out. From my house I could walk to the train station, catch a train to London Waterloo, tube to St Pancras and then train again to the centre of Brussels, Metro to my friends place. If I flew, I'd walk to the station, train it to London Waterloo, tube then train to Gatwick, have all the security hassle and waiting around there, fly to Brussels Zevantem, metro to my friends house. Given that I like trains, it was a simple decision for me. I don't know if it was cheaper or not because cost was not my primary concern, but convenience was. Flying is a horrible experience nowadays, with airlines treating travellers like cattle. Once it was great, but I'd only fly long-haul now. The rail alternatives are so much more comfortable.

Question: What would have happened if the allies dropped thousands of men into Central Paris and Berlin and also the concentration camps, instead of invading Normandy?

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Were the women from older generation really as unhappy and oppressed as modern feminists report?
Answer: It was certainly much more common in the past than in today's enlightened times. This makes the story of my mother all the more surprising. She was born in south London in 1920. Her family was working class, and her father, my grandfather, was quick with his fists. My mother also dropped heavy hints that he was a sexual abuser. Anyway, she left home when she was just sixteen possibly for this reason, and worked as a furrier. During WW2 she had many boyfriends and enjoyed herself. She was a member of the Communist Party for a brief period, and worked with refugees, which is how she met my Dad. When she married my father in 1953 she joined him in the family business. They had a furniture shop in Camden Town, north London, and then two, then three, then four and always she worked together with him in the open, unheated shops. Although my brother and I were born, she split her time between work and family and built up a good business, diversifying into contract furnishing, carpets, kitchens and property. She wanted to work and was good at it. If you had called her 'oppressed' she would have laughed. She laughed a lot, and was a pretty strong woman despite being barely 5' tall. She was bright and quick, and had a very strong independent streak that modern women would recognise. She knew how to juggle before it was a thing. She was a very practical woman with a strong instinct for survival. My father was unfaithful and not as discreet as was wise, but she decided that the family and prosperous business was more important than his weakness, so she tolerated it as long as he didn't humiliate her. When she was 70 (he as ten years younger then her) he committed them to a disastrous business deal that ruined them. It revealed the extent of his extra-marital activities, and she left him. It takes guts to start again at that age, but she was very strong. She led a happy, contented, independent life until dying in her sleep aged 87. Before assuming all women in the past were drudges, realise they were all individuals. My mother was not a stay-at-home mum. She was a business woman, a mother, a truck driver, a scuba diver, a horse rider, a one-time political activist, a charity worker, a painter and a woman of her time. Just not the conventional type.

Question: What is the weirdest thing that's ever happened to you at a bar?
Answer: In the early 1970's when I was about 18, I drove from London to Scotland with my cousin from NY and a mate of mine. We got as far north as Skye. It was a fun road trip. Heading home, we stopped for a drink in a pub in Glencoe. When I ordered our drinks at the bar (in my London accent), I noticed a curious quiet. The usual bonhomie we had found everywhere in Scotland was strangely absent. There were some sideways glances directed at us too, and we felt rather uncomfortable. We were a bit mystified, so we drank up and left. In 1692, 30 members of the MacDonald clan had been murdered there by forces loyal to the English crown. They have long memories in Glencoe

Question: What is a good place to live for families who want to be near nature but also close to London for work? Can you explain why you chose this place?
Answer: St Albans is good. The Thameslink train service gets you in to St Pancras in 20–25 minutes. I used that line daily for over twenty years and it's pretty good. St Albans is in Hertfordshire and there's a 1000-year old cathedral there. The schools are great and you're surrounded by green belt. Property prices aren't cheap though, so £750k + for a four bed house is what you'd need to expect. If that's too much, Luton is overlooked. It's two stops up the rail line from St Albans, so slightly further out from London, but prices are much lower. It's more blue-collar and gets a bad rap, but access is superb (M1, airport, rail), there are some real property gems to be had. We lived there for 16 years in this house where we brought up our children. They went to really good schools in Harpenden, well into the Waitrose Belt and half way between Luton and St Albans. Question: Will I lose weight easier if I fight against wanting too much food?
Answer: In my experience, getting a grip on my food craving is pretty essential if I want to shed weight or maintain it. This is because I love food, and would over eat if I let myself. So self discipline is for me at least, a necessity. We are all different and you may not have a big appetite. But being careful about what you eat and portion control are both essential, whether it's getting yourself to eat more or less. I am pretty used to my self discipline so it's easy for me, but my brother, who was overweight all his life, found it terribly difficult and never really mastered it.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Is sweating a reliable method for weight loss? How much does it contribute to reducing body fat percentage?
Answer: Sweating itself just means you just lose water. Water weighs 1kg per litre, so if you weigh yourself before and after going in a sauna, sure, you'll be lighter. However you'll also be thirsty, so as soon as you glug down some water, you'll put weight back on. If you do some vigorous exercise that gets a good sweat up and do it regularly over a period of time, providing you are on a balanced diet and watch portion size, you'll probably genuinely lose weight.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Are dancers really "constantly on a diet" as it is often portrayed?
Answer: Female ballet dancers are under pressure to be easy to lift, so of course their weight is important. However it's also true that they are expected to fit into an aesthetic that requires them to look slight and lithe. Dancers are no different to athletes in many respects. They tend to be all born with certain physical attributes that make them suitable for their very specialised jobs. So no one who is naturally a bit on the average side weight-wise would stand a chance of getting a job with a dance company. Only the naturally thin, small ones even stand a chance. On top of that, dancing at a professional level is all about control. Ballet dancers are masters of it, and can make their bodies bend to their considerable will. So they need to lose a few pounds after the summer break? It's done in a week. Dancers are not particularly well rewarded for their work, yet the ones I knew were all super-dedicated. They were all very focussed. A combination of being born with the right look, the desire to dance and do what is necessary and an iron will means that "constantly on a diet" doesn't really mean anything. They are in the right aesthetically zone already and most of them wouldn't even really notice 'being on a diet'.

Question: How do I determine which country is my primary citizenship if I am a dual citizen of the US and another country?
Answer: Dunno. It's up to you. I have two citizenships, and it's fairly easy for me. I choose the country of my birth and the one whose culture I most identify with as my primary one, if I have to choose, but I don't see why I'd have to. It's hypothetical.

Question: I want to apply for dual citizenship but in my birth certificate, my parents’ birth date is different than their birth date on their birth certificate. What should I do?

Anyway, I got my citizenship and passport.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: Why do the British say "I need the loo" instead of "I need to use the restroom"?
Answer: British people are less direct than American, are no strangers to euphemisms and are terrified of embarrassment. It's therefore odd that we are more direct about normal bodily functions. Surely we should be the ones still saying "I need to spend a penny" or "Where is the smallest room in the house?", but by and large in this instance, nowadays we Brits call a spade a spade. It is Americans who struggle with alluding even indirectly to the lavatory, preferring to pretend they need a lie down rather than a sit down. Why?. It may have something to do with the changing manners in the post war period in Britain. There was a time in living memory, when people stopped in the street and removed their hats when hearses drove past, when people were friends for years called each other "Mr" or "Mrs", when men wore ties to do the gardening at weekends. I'm not ancient, but I remember these things, and I've noticed they (and many other conventions) have all gone, and more casual conventions have taken over. These class barriers were time-consuming and elaborate and we largely just didn't have time for them any more. Domains that were once considered "working class" are now the realm of all classes and some have even become 'gentrified'…think of popular music, once considered 'common', nowadays the members of a band are likely to have first met at public school or uni (Coldplay, Pink Floyd etc, etc). Swearing is permitted, with certain exceptions…no one clutches their pearls if someone says "bloody" any more. We all watch the same TV (or stream it), abuse the same substances and go to similar places on holiday. Class, and with it, language, has blurrier edges. It's become cool to be working class and even coarse. So Brits have moved in one direction. Can the same be said of Americans? I don't know for sure, but I think not.

Name: Nick Schön
Question: How can I determine the right portion size to avoid weight gain?
Answer: I was interested in this too recently, and I remembered the old German "FDH" (Friss die Hälfte) diet. Basically, eat half what you normally eat. Just literally cut that steak in half, have only one egg and one slice of toast instead of two. I didn't cheat. I felt surprisingly satisfied although the portions looked paltry. I ate more slowly to compensate, and that meany I gave my stomach time to fill. I drank more water to space out the mouthfuls. I found that half of what I normally consume was too little and I lost weight, but a small amount more than that was adequate for me to maintain my weight. Question: Why did Britain after WW2 fail to become a big industrial power like Germany and Japan?
Answer: Britain did become a great industrial power after WW2, but squandered the opportunities it had. It is certainly true that Britain had been badly bombed, but that largely stopped by 1942. In the case of Germany, the bombing was tragic and continued en masse until 1945. No town was left in damaged, no city left intact. Everything, including the transport network was in tatters. That gave it to opportunity to 'build back better'. Germany received 11% of the Marshal Plan. Britain got 26%, but didn't invest it in the same way the new Federal government in West Germany did. In the latter, companies were not simply given handouts to build new factories. They could borrow it at a rate of interest, which meant the government had an increasing capital sum to lend. The result was that companies who were best at identifying markets and where to invest, had control. For instance, Volkswagen rebuilt their factories in Wolfsburg (once it was returned by the British who could see no merit in the Beetle). The term "economic miracle" was first coined in 1950. British manufacturing could manage without large scale rebuilding, which meant that by 1960 for instance, pre-war factories and work practices were still being used. Whereas German unions were represented on Boards, this was famously not the case in Britain, where class-based industrial relations hobbled the entire country for many decades. It turned out that there was a distinct advantage to creating a modern country from scratch in the mid 20th century. Germany in effect, played a bad hand extremely well. Britain had a better hand but played it terribly. The question really should be how did Britain manage so well, given its state post war?

Question: What problem did you solve in a creative way?
Answer: We (the ad agency I was working for) had a client who owned lots of poster (billboard) sites. They wanted us (my writer at the time, Peter and me) to solve their problem: how to test the effectiveness of their sites so that they could present a strong case to people wishing to book them. The problem was that if we ran an ad for a real product, that would naturally contaminate the findings, based on whether people liked that brand or not. So we decided to invent an imaginary product…run a couple of posters for it in a particular location, and then ask people about it to see how effective it had been. We came up with “Mr Wiggley’s Worms”. It was satisfyingly niche and unique, and since we came up with the brand one afternoon after a good lunch, we knew no one would have heard of it. Apparently it worked very well. Anglers were going into fishing shops and asking for “A tin of Mr Wiggley’s please” to the utter consternation of the shopkeepers. I was told that some enterprising individuals even tried to copy the tin and launch the brand based on the free advertising. Can’t believe they ever hoped to make their fortune, but who knows? Anyway, the client got the data they wanted and was very happy, and the poster won us a creative award that year.

Question: Is being a ballerina or ballet dancer a financially stable career? Do dancers have time for other activities outside of dancing?
Answer: For a tiny percentage of dancers at the peak of the industry I suppose so, but most dancers have to compete for contracts on an annual basis. Unless you live and work in a big city with several ballet companies, a failure to get a new contract will mean moving home to somewhere else. My late wife danced professionally in Germany for ten years, during which time she danced for five companies in five different towns. Luckily she could drive and they were all close together (except for one) so we only moved three times. In every occasion she moved to work with a better company. Her choice. I earned more than half our joint income, and nearly all the other dancers we knew either had partners or shared accommodation. She was the only married dancer of either gender we encountered. After that, she moved into teaching which is not very well paid, and then examining for the Royal Academy of Dance. That isn't a road to riches either, but she was sent to China, Brazil, India, South Africa, the USA, Italy, Scotland, Mexico and a lot of other places for a month at a time on full expenses. The pay wasn't great, but it was fun at least. Here she is (with the hat and elephant) on tour in India. Some things money can't buy.
